items.heading: 동등정리와한계
items.text:
[PDF page 3]
1. Ricardian equivalence 
• Take the budget constraint of a representative consumer. 
Assume lump sum taxes, Tt. Assume the consumer can hold his wealth 
in either an asset A (which can be capital, shares, private bonds,..) and 
government bonds, B: 
Bt+1 + At+1 = WtNt + Πt − Tt − Ct + (1 + Rt)Bt + (1 + RAt)At 
• Consider the budget constraint of the government. 
The government collects (lump sum) taxes Tt, spends Gt, and ﬁnances 
the diﬀerence by issuing debt: 
Bt+1 − Bt = (Gt − Tt) + RtBt 
Nr. 3
Cite as: Olivier Blanchard, course materials for 14.452 Macroeconomic Theory II, Spring 2007.  
MIT OpenCourseWare (http://ocw.mit.edu/), Massachusetts Institute of Technology. Downloaded on [DD Month YYYY]. 


[PDF page 4]
Replace the government budget in the consumer’s budget constraint to get: 
At+1 = WtNt + Πt − Gt − Ct + (1 + RAt)At 
Note that the budget constraint depends on Gt but does not depend on either 
Bt or Tt. This is the Ricardian equivalence proposition: 
• For a given sequence of government spending, changes in the timing of 
lump sum taxes have no eﬀect on the allocation. 
• Equivalently: If the government saves less by decreasing Tt, consumers 
will save more in exactly the same amount. Total saving (private plus 
public saving) will be unaﬀected. 
• Equivalently: If the government increases the deﬁcit by decreasing Tt 
and issues debt, consumers will be willing to hold this additional debt 
at the same interest rate. 
• Equivalently: Debt will not crowd out capital accumulation. 
Nr. 4
Cite as: Olivier Blanchard, course materials for 14.452 Macroeconomic Theory II, Spring 2007.  
MIT OpenCourseWare (http://ocw.mit.edu/), Massachusetts Institute of Technology. Downloaded on [DD Month YYYY]. 


[PDF page 5]
The obvious limits of the relevance of Ricardian equivalence. 
• Finite horizons. Consider a decrease in Tt. Suppose some consumers do 
not expect to be there when taxes are increased. Then the decrease in 
Tt leads to a positive wealth eﬀect. 
They will increase consumption and thus not increase saving by as much 
as the decrease in taxes. Debt will have an eﬀect on the allocation. 
(Diamond OLG, or Blanchard-Yaari). Empirical importance? 
• Liquidity or cash constraints. If for some consumers, Ct ≤ WtNt +Πt − 
Tt, then clearly changes in taxes will matter. 
Need to understand the exact nature of the liquidity constraint. 
• Bounded rationality. Tax increases may be far in the future, and not be 
taken into account. Horizon does matter. 
• Distortionary taxes. 
Nr. 5
